results.name: Impacts of cover cropping on soil health in an Urban farm in the MidSouth
results.description: There is a major push toward accelerating the understanding of carbon sequestration processes to mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from soil.  Given that agricultural practices are a major source of GHGs, there has been much research into how agricultural management regimes might improve carbon sequestration in soils in support of long-term carbon sequestration benefits. One management strategy to improve soil health and GHG capture in agriculture is the use of cover crops. Cover crops have been showed to increase organic carbon stocks in soils but there are major knowledge gaps in cover crops facilitate these carbon stock increases, specifically the mechanisms by which cover crops generate recalcitrate soil organic matter and alter soil pore structure, all of which can be elucidated by the coupled FTICR, XCT, and metagenomes MONet will provide. This proposed work will expand our understanding of soil ecosystem processes associated with cover crops utilization, particularly in the MidSouth region of the United States where there are few studies on soil processes in agriculturally relevant systems. This work will support my ongoing research on plant-microbial interface dynamics in MidSouth agricultural systems. This work will provide crucial data in support of future initiatives on prescriptive cover crop usage based on field conditions. I propose samples from an ongoing cover crop experiment in an urban farm in Memphis TN, which tests soil microbiome and soil health effects across a soil moisture gradient with different cover cropping combinations. I propose nine samples, three from control plots (no cover crops), three from a treatment consisting of the cover crops Tillage Radish, Winter Peak and Winter Triticale, and three from a treatment consisting of Forage Turnips, Crimson Clover and Winter Rye.
results.title: Impacts of cover cropping on soil health in an Urban farm in the MidSouth

results.name: Farming for more than food: Cultivation and management's influence on soil biogeochemical properties
results.description:
More than half the land in the United States is in agriculture, and while we know how to produce the maximum crop yield from this land in the short term, recently increasing emphasis has been placed on benefits like carbon storage and bolstering soil health. However, the methods for achieving these emerging goals have yet to be fully understood and must be determined by scientific data. This proposal seeks to help fill this knowledge gap by applying the data collected through the MONet program, including organic matter molecular composition and soil microstructural measurements, to samples collected at the Farming Systems Project (FSP) at Beltsville Agricultural Research Center.

FSP was created to quantify differences between yield and nutrient management between organic and conventional farming systems. FSP was initiated in 1993 and now contains five treatments in conjunction with a forest control site. The treatments include no-till, chisel-till, and organic 2/3/6-year rotations. The rotations are summarized as follows with rye and vetch being cover crops, 1) no-till, a 3-year rotation of corn-rye-soybean-wheat/soybean, 2) chisel-till, a 3-year rotation of corn-rye-soybean-wheat/soybean, 3) organic 2-year, corn-rye-soybean-vetch and rye, 4) organic 3-year, corn-rye-soybean-wheat-vetch and rye, 5) organic 6-year, corn-rye-soybean-wheat-alfalfa-alfalfa-alfalfa, 6) forest site, predominantly red maple and white oak. The no-till and chisel-till receive synthetic fertilizer. The organic systems receive manure and legumes as fertilizer and annual tillage. 

The long-term studies conducted at FSP have shown that soil carbon and nitrogen concentrations change depending on agricultural management. However, our capabilities only extend to measuring total carbon and nitrogen pools through dry combustion. Leveraging the FSP soils with the analysis conducted by MONet will give deeper insight into how agricultural management alters the composition of organic matter, the pore network structure, geochemistry, and the microbial community's diversity and function. 

The data collected through MONet will add valuable information to my group's current research project, which seeks to measure the difference in soil carbon and nitrogen associated with specific mineral pools in each treatment through selective extractions. Furthermore, there are a multitude of collaborators in government and academia with ongoing projects at FSP who will also benefit from the MONet analyses. FSP is an invaluable resource for cross-disciplinary research and is heavily used in agricultural model development and validation. The comprehensive dataset generated through sampling the FSP sites with MONet will be valuable across many ongoing research projects. Additionally, we plan to use this first proposal as a preliminary sampling to refine the research questions and sampling sites in a Large Scope proposal and our future research. Characterizing the FSP soils across agricultural management is a unique opportunity to apply the robust MONET analyses to start answering how the predominant land use in the United States alters the life-sustaining soil.
results.title: Farming for more than food: Cultivation and management's influence on soil biogeochemical properties

results.name: Organic Matter and Microplastics in Biosolids Amended Soils
results.description: Our objectives are to determine how long-term applications of biosolids will affect soil organic carbon, soil structure, soil hydraulic and microbiological characteristics. The overarching question is whether long-term applications of biosolids to soil provide a sustainable alternative to commercial fertilizers for agricultural production. In addition, we are investigating the transfer of microplastics from biosolids to soils and how microplastics will affect overall soil health. The field-site is a unique site in the dryland Pacific Northwest where biosolids from Seattle have been applied for the past 23 years and we have monitored nutrients, organic matter, and yields over time. The site is under no-till, so any structural changes of the soil can directly be attributed to biosolids applications. We have established a replicated, randomized block design experiment at this site where we are comparing three rates of biosolids applications, a no-fertilizer control, and an inorganic fertilizer control. We will take soil samples from each of the 5 experimental treatments. The site is also part of the Soil Health Institute's long-term monitoring sites.
results.title: Organic Matter and Microplastics in Biosolids Amended Soils

results.name: Czarnecki MONet Request
results.description:
Peatlands are carbon sinks that store approximately 1/3rd of global soil carbon, while comprising only 1/30th of the total land area. This carbon is vulnerable to oxidation due to climate change and anthropogenic manipulation, such as drainage. While the assumption remains that in drier and more oxic conditions, decomposition increases, there remains uncertainty surrounding the roles of biological and biogeochemical feedbacks in the decomposition dynamics of northern peatland ecosystems. Here we propose a study across a transect between a drained and unaltered peatland to better understand these dynamics. 
Our site in northern Minnesota, is an acidic, nutrient poor, Sphagnum dominated peatland, that was ditched for drainage in the 1910’s for agricultural purposes. As you move away from the ditch, you transition from a now tree-dominated, forested peatland to a ‘pristine’ open peatland dominated by sedge and ericaceous shrub. This ‘pristine’ open peatland is representative of our drained site, pre-drainage. In prior studies conducted at this site, a shift in microbial abundance was observed, from ericoid mycorrhizal fungi in the ‘pristine’ peat to ectomycorrhizal fungi at the drain site. This transition was observed along with a decrease in peat C:N (more eutrophic) and an increase in peat humification at the drained site. 
The ectomycorrhizal fungi found at the site are believed to be associated with the roots of the trees found at the site (P. mariana and L. laricina) and are capable of producing ligninolytic peroxidases, enzymes that are capable of breaking down complex lignin compounds. We hypothesize that the enzymatic processes associated with ectomycorrhizal fungi, primarily peroxidases, are responsible for the observed degradation at the drained site. Additionally, we hypothesize that the symbiotic relationships between ericoid mycorrhizal fungi and Sphagnum creates a symbiotic relationship where nutrients are recycled, preventing saprotrophs from scavenging in our ‘pristine’ site, and slowing decomposition rates. The absence of this symbiotic relationship in the drained site will result in an increase of nutrient availability (primarily nitrogen). High-resolution molecular composition of soil organic matter data will be used in tandem with metagenomic data and enzymatic activity to understand how peatland carbon storage has been affected by long-term drainage. Geochemistry and soil organic matter compositional data will also give insight into understanding how these changes will alter nutrient cycling in peatlands.
results.title: Czarnecki MONet Request

results.name: Scott MONet Request.
results.description: The University of Georgia (UGA) campus houses a diverse community of tree species that benefit the campus community by mitigating air pollution, sequestering carbon, reducing energy costs, and providing aesthetic, mental, and emotional benefits. The UGA Grounds Department oversees tree healthcare, pruning, pest control, and irrigation management, still, many of the trees experience stressors including compaction, limited soil area, light interference, and elevated temperatures. An urban disturbance gradient will be created by categorizing trees into different levels based on soil area and compaction. Ten tree species (five ectomycorrhizal, five endomycorrhizal) were selected on UGA’s campus to investigate the impact of urban disturbance and mycorrhizal association on soil organic matter quality and nutrient cycling. We propose to collect six sampling sets from trees on the campus during December. Our understanding of tree stress is limited by our understanding of soil biogeochemical, microbial, and physical processes that are altered by urban disturbances. This research will assist in making predictions on soil C stocks and quality in urban soils, whose role in the global carbon cycle is challenging to study due to high heterogeneity and difficulty in sampling urban environments. By participating in the MONet soil program, we will have a more detailed understanding of the specific below-ground challenges that our study trees are experiencing. The findings from this study will provide valuable insight to urban foresters, land managers, and scientists, by quantifying the relative importance of compaction and soil area on overall tree condition and soil biogeochemical processes.
results.title: Scott MONet Request.

results.name: Exploring Root-Mediated Greenhouse Gas Dynamics in Bottomland Forests Amid Climate and Hydrological Change
results.description:
Our primary scientific objective is to examine how aboveground and belowground roots influence greenhouse gas cycling in mineral soil bottomland forests (BHFs) in response to climate change and hydrologic variability. Toward this larger goal, we propose three hypotheses: (i) initial porosity affects root location and density, but later root growth drives a positive feedback that promotes structure and porosity development which in turn facilitates gas transport, (ii) soil nutrient “hot spots” (NHS) are a first-order control on the belowground root density and rhizosphere chemistry, and (iii) high bald cypress knee density (i.e., knee islands) lowers the need for fungal associates, whereas low knee density have more mycelia that seek out nutrients. Using a synergistic Modeling-Experimentation (Mod-Ex) approach we will test these hypotheses by (1) examining how the physical, biogeochemical, and mineralogical properties of the soil vary in the presence and absence of knee islands, (2) investigating how resource distribution, rooting density, and redox potential affect net methane (CH4) fluxes and methanogenic and methanotrophic communities, and (3) test how scale transition theory can be implemented into model representations of these landscapes, while also running model tests of system uncertainty to inform field and experimental data collection efforts.

By participating in the MONet soil program, we will be able to achieve these goals through the submission of six sample sets from sites that vary in landscape position (3 knee island vs. 3 non-knee island) along floodplain back channels that are occupied by bald cypress. DNA, FTICR and XCT data obtained through MONet will help us achieve our research goal above. Our work will improve understanding of ecosystem services through the modeling of CH4 dynamics across BHF watersheds, using information gained during field and lab (MONet) measurements and mesocosm experiments.
results.title: Exploring Root-Mediated Greenhouse Gas Dynamics in Bottomland Forests Amid Climate and Hydrological Change

results.name: Before It's Gone: Comparisons of Soil Chacateristics in Glaciated and Non Glaciated Catchments
results.description:
Alpine systems are fragile and small changes have wide-ranging impacts on downstream ecological communities. Changes in hydrology caused by a warming climate and the loss of glaciers will have significant impacts on sediment transport and biogeochemical fluxes to downstream ecosystems. Glacier National Park (GNP) spans 4,080 km2 of the northwestern mountainous region of Montana near southern Alberta and British Columbia, Canada and in the context of the fading cryosphere GNP provides a prime location to conduct a watershed study of alpine glacial systems. Significant glacier retreat has been occurring at Grinnell Glacier since 1950, making it an iconic symbol of climate change.  Due to the urgent nature of understanding a disappearing ecological system, we have collected physical, hydraulic, and biological data from both Grinnell Glacier and Cataract Creek Valley watersheds over the summers of 2021-2023. 
These paired watersheds provide a robust contrast between a currently glaciated and a previously glaciated watershed catchment.  We have a research permit to collect samples and develop a 2D sediment transport model (HEC-RAS) that integrates flow regimes, environmental conditions, and the movement of particulates through these systems. Combining data from the USGS’s Montana LiDAR Inventory with in situ acoustic doppler profiling we can model the movement of carbon and the microbial community, both planktonic and sediment attached, through these alpine systems. 
Adding the data from a MONet project to this effort will greatly enhance our understanding of what constituents from upstream soils potentially contribute to the material transported down valley (e.g., organic matter, phosphorous, nitrogen, and sediment).  It is important to note that the proposed soil cores are not in permafrost or frozen during the summer sampling months. We will be able to compare our microbial community and geochemistry data collected from each watershed from increasing stream order and watershed complexity (project ongoing) with that from the soil data collected from this proposed MONet project and data from other alpine systems. The combination of surface water hydrologic modeling, microbial ecology and soil characterization will provide novel insight to the impacts of glacier loss and changes in runoff regimes to downstream ecological communities and ecosystem services.
results.title: Before It's Gone: Comparisons of Soil Chacateristics in Glaciated and Non Glaciated Catchments

results.name: DeVan MONet Request
results.description:
Aridlands comprise over a third of Earth's terrestrial surface and contribute substantially to global interannual variability of carbon fluxes (IAV). Despite their importance, aridlands are poorly represented in ecosystem models, even as models predict global expansion of these regions. Moreover, the Desert Southwest ecoregion is currently absent in MONet. In the Southwestern US, carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) dynamics have pulse-driven responses triggered by episodic summer monsoon rains. The summer monsoon generally coincides with microbially relevant phenological shifts that likely impact ecosystem processes and help explain high IAV. This proposal aims to explore how seasonal water availability and associated phenological shifts affect microbial activity and nutrient cycling in relation to ecosystem productivity and respiration currently being measured by eddy covariance flux towers. 

Sampling will occur at three AmeriFlux sites associated with the Sevilleta Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) program, located in the Desert Southwest ecoregion in central New Mexico. These sites encompass three distinct dryland ecoregions vulnerable to climate change, including two grasslands and a shrubland, each with distinct net ecosystem exchange dynamics. MONet-supported sampling before, during, and after the summer monsoon will enable capture of pulse-driven fluctuations in soil physical, chemical, and biological properties, thereby improving understanding of belowground contributions to ecosystem functioning.  We will integrate MONet and AmeriFlux data to provide insights into pulse-driven microbial C and N dynamics, alongside other variables like soil CO2, temperature, and other microbial sequencing projects occurring at the Sevilleta LTER. Our collaboration with AmeriFlux and LTER ensures our commitment to provide publicly available data for future research pursuits.
results.title: DeVan MONet Request

results.name: Umpqua National Forest Postfire
results.description:
Sampling on the Umpqua National Forest will allow land managers to assess the effects of severe wildfire and postfire management on soil physical, chemical, and biological properties that the Forest Service could not otherwise measure. We will compare properties in severely burned soils within and outside salvage logging units, and in areas with low or no soil burn severity. Understanding which properties changed in our local burned soils, and by how much, will help National Forest soil scientists and silviculturists refine best management practices for burned soils. The results of this work could affect the amount of organic material retained or added to burned areas following future fires, for example, with the goals of helping soil microbial communities and organic matter recover and minimizing structural changes and erosion.
The sampling sites are already being monitored for visible signs of erosion, but more information is needed to 
understand how severely the chemical and biological soil properties were impacted in areas mapped as high soil burn severity in postfire rapid assessment. Also, federal staff and public land users are increasingly interested in potential impacts of land management on soil microbial communities, and MONet analyses will provide the first microbial community data on the Umpqua National Forest to form a baseline for discussing potential impacts.
Data from recently burned soils will also help the MONet dataset represent a prevalent disturbance in forest soils and support including wildfire impacts in soil process models. Fire effects are an important component of all ecological processes in the extensive seasonally dry forests of western North America and similar biomes worldwide.
results.title: Umpqua National Forest Postfire

results.name: Soil changes across a short rotation woody crop chronosequence in the southeastern US
results.description: The southeastern United States has great potential to grow short rotation woody crops like eastern cottonwood for biomass and bioenergy including feedstocks for sustainable aviation fuels due to its favorable climate, timber industry, and available land resources. While bioenergy crops have potential to replace fossil fuels, they can also provide ecosystem services including soil carbon sequestration. Production costs of hybrid poplar grown on 2-3 year coppice rotations for biomass feedstock are still prohibitively high for wide-spread adoption, although calculations have often ignored co-produced ecosystem services relative to alternative land uses. Ecosystem services of hybrid poplar on short rotations have the potential to diversify income streams for landowners and producers and reduce impacts of market volatility risks while providing additional benefits to society. Belowground carbon sequestration, in particular, could be provided by all landowners growing short rotation woody crop plantations, however carbon accrual rates need to be quantified and a mechanistic understanding of soil carbon processes in short rotation woody crop fields needs to better understood, so that it can be incorporated into process-based models. Therefore, the goals of our study are to look at how soil properties change as short rotation woody crops are growing and replacing traditional row crop agriculture. We would sample at a field site where we have a poplar plantation that was planted in 2019 and another one nearby that was planted in 2021. Additionally, we would look at soils from two different eastern cottonwood genotypes that have been shown to have differing physiology and nitrogen use efficiency. We would also sample from adjacent agricultural soils to get a baseline condition. Although we are currently measuring soil parameters such as soil carbon and nitrogen concentrations, participation in the MONet soil program will allow us to look more deeply at soil microbial communities and processes to better understand the mechanisms by which soil communities are changing as poplar production occurs on these sites and how tree physiology and genetic variability impacts soil communities. These data also allows us to compare soil microbial communities and functioning with other parameters that we have been monitoring at our field sites including yearly soil carbon accrual, aboveground tree productivity, soil respiration rates, and trace gas (nitrous oxide, methane) emissions. In total, integrating ecosystem services into short rotation poplar production will benefit a variety of stakeholder groups. For researchers and biomass industry, these data will introduce greater confidence in future projections and further enable comparison with other energy crop systems where similar metrics are presented. For agricultural producers, short rotation woody crops provide the opportunity to effectively utilize marginal land, diversify outputs and take advantage of income from the energy sector and retain it in the local economy. In addition, rural landowners may benefit from ecosystem service credits based on carbon sequestration and/or water quality improvement. In total, incorporating ecosystem services from hybrid poplar compared to alternate land uses may be an essential component of meeting targets of $3/GGE (gallon of gasoline equivalent) and less for biofuels.
results.title: Soil changes across a short rotation woody crop chronosequence in the southeastern US

results.name: Rhizosphere microfluidics and organic carbon chemistry reflect the migration of tidal freshwater wetlands
results.description: Rhizosphere biogeochemistry in tidal freshwater wetlands is poorly understood, especially under dynamic shifts in vegetation composition. Here, we focus on a tidal freshwater wetland in the Chesapeake Bay watershed, where accelerated sea level rise over the last decade has driven transitions between Zizania aquatica (wild rice), Typha spp. (cattail), and unvegetated mudflats. Expanding mudflat areas and inland migration of Typha threaten wild rice, a critical food source for local and migrating birds. Wild rice is a unique bioindicator species that is highly sensitive to environmental perturbations. It is an annual plant and has finer, more complex, roots/rhizomes compared to Typha. Overarching Objective: Examine how recent shifts in vegetation correspond to differences in soil biogeochemical characteristics, then use this data to enhance wild rice restoration and develop new microfluidic platforms to study the wetland rhizosphere (i.e., a wetland rhizosphere on a chip). Research Questions: (a) Does wild rice have a higher degree of physical and hydraulic complexity in the rhizosphere channel/pore network compared to cattail? This can be addressed with XCT measurements and insight from SFTEL/computing. (b) Do wild rice and cattail display differences in soil microbial lipidomic profiles and organic C chemistry in the rhizosphere? This can be addressed with omics, and FTICR and TOC measurements, respectively. (c) Following loss of vegetation cover, how different is mudflat soil (by XCT, omics, FTICR) compared to soils with standing wild rice and cattail – do soil organic molecules in mudflats have higher mass and lower nominal oxidation state of C (NOSC) compared to under living vegetation? Knowledge Advancement: (1) Insights into how sea level rise alters biogeochemical cycling in tidal freshwater wetlands, (2) how specific features of the soil channel/pore network, the microbiome function, and the organic chemistry help explain wild rice recovery, and (3) how microfluidic platforms could better mimic the rhizosphere of tidal freshwater wetlands to test fine-scale soil processes.
results.title: Rhizosphere microfluidics and organic carbon chemistry reflect the migration of tidal freshwater wetlands

results.name: Investigating the Biogeochemical Importance of Alpine Wetlands at Niwot Ridge
results.description:
This project will evaluate the biogeochemical importance of three different alpine wetland ecosystems located at the Niwot Ridge Long-Term Ecological Research site. This work will help us better predict these ecosystems’ responses to impacts of global climate change, including increases in anthropogenic-driven nutrient deposition.

Wetland sites support high rates of biogeochemical cycling compared to surrounding alpine environments, mainly due to changes in oxygen availability and a greater availability of nutrients (i.e., nitrogen and carbon) that support redox reactions. Though they are key control points on the landscape, few studies have characterized the biogeochemistry at these sites. Characterization is needed to understand how wetland types will be impacted by the changing environment; especially in these more climate- sensitive alpine environments.

By participating in the MONet soil program we will gain biogeochemical insight into three types of wetlands our group has previously studied; alpine wet meadows, solifluction lobes and subalpine wetlands. Our group has investigated porewater chemistry, soil physicochemical properties, and sulfur reaction rates at these sites. We can compare the findings from MONet to analyses from previous field seasons, thus giving us insights into temporal changes at these sites. We also plan to take additional gas measurements (carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide) and redox measurements (electron shuttling capacity) in tandem with MONet sampling.

Participating in MONet will strengthen the suite of biogeochemical data available to researchers working at Niwot Ridge. Data will be shared within Niwot’s database and contribute to MONet’s mission of a “FAIR” approach to soil science data across the United States. We plan to publish these results as summarizing the importance of these often-understudied ecosystems with six early-career researchers leading this effort.
results.title: Investigating the Biogeochemical Importance of Alpine Wetlands at Niwot Ridge

results.name: Evans KBS MONet Request
results.description: We propose to sample the agricultural land use gradient at KBS Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) site to understand how agricultural management affects soil molecular properties. Interactions between soil biological and soil physical properties (including X-ray CT on intact soil) are a major gap in our understanding of soil health. MONet measurements across our long-term gradient of land uses will help fill this gap, and advance our ability to link soil measurements to management decisions (tillage, cover crops, perennials), and ecosystem service outcomes (soil health, trace gas flux, soil carbon accumulation). Samples will come from 6 long-term treatments in KBS’s “Main Cropping Systems Experiment” (https://lter.kbs.msu.edu/research/long-term-experiments/main-cropping-system-experiment/), oriented along a land use intensity gradient: four treatments in row crop agriculture, corn-soy-wheat rotation: 1) Conventional with tillage, 2) No-tillage 3) Reduced input (1/3 of chemical inputs), with cover crops 4) Organic, with no chemical inputs and cover crops. There are also two successional plant communities, 5) Early successional grassland, and 6) Deciduous forest, both of which will serve as references to row crop agriculture. Because of high spatial variation in early successional grassland (high plant diversity), we will sample an additional plot (N=5) in this treatment. This will not exceed 24 samples because forest plots have only 3 field replicates. The KBS LTER is funded by NSF through 2028 and has adequate resources and personnel to collect/ship samples and publish results. Previous and current data on soils, climate, and ecosystem services generated by the KBS LTER (https://lter.kbs.msu.edu/datatables) will increase the impact of this work. For instance, no-till treatments have accumulated greater soil organic matter than conventional tilled treatments and have greater water holding capacity. Micro-scale molecular measurements may inform mechanisms. While various soil pore and amplicon sequencing data have been generated on 1-2 treatments at a time, there has been no previous study characterizing more than two treatments in the gradient at a time, with both structural and biological data. Such data will help us understand how variation in these properties links to soil function and ecosystem services. The long-term (35 year) nature of these treatments, in addition to the existing resources and datasets, make this a unique opportunity.
results.title: Evans KBS MONet Request

results.name: Assessing the bioweathering of minerals along a bioclimate gradient
results.description:
The weathering of silicate minerals contributes towards soil development and plays an integral role in the global carbon cycle by influencing climate stabilization (i.e., carbon fixation and sequestration) and the geochemical factors that regulate soil carbon distribution. Microorganisms accelerate weathering reactions and are fundamental in the release and biogeochemical cycling of rock-bound essential nutrients and metals. However, the contribution of biologically mediated mineral transformations to these processes is understudied and underestimated in climate models and soil carbon stock estimations, particularly within forested ecosystems. 

Our research will examine how climate and nutrient availability influence mineral weathering along a bioclimatic gradient in the perhumid coastal temperate rainforests of southeast Alaska. This extreme environment represents an intense mineral weathering regime facilitated by highly productive forests coupled with a humid-maritime climate, driving some of the fastest rates of soil development, soil organic carbon (SOC) accumulation, and plant succession in the world.  

Data collected through the MONet initiative will support multiple funded proposals including a DOE EMSL Large Scale Research Proposal and research funding provided by the USDA Forest Service through a Cooperative Agreement. Our team is focused on employing field- and lab-based analysis techniques to differentiate biotic and abiotic weathering agents, identify incipient weathering features, and quantify elemental loss in minerals transformed through biotic-mineral interactions (i.e., fungal hyphae, biofilms) via the use of high-resolution microscopy, mass spectrometry, and elemental analysis. Specifically, fungal-accessible and fungal-excluding mesh bags containing unreacted ground rock of contrasting essential element abundance were deployed in the field along a north-south bioclimate sequence spanning three study areas of contrasting landscape age near Juneau, AK: Mendenhall Glacier (1805 mm/yr.), Taku Harbor (2711 mm/yr.), and Prince of Wales Island (3191 mm/yr.). These field locations will address our objectives through variations in precipitation, vegetation, and soil development, including the degree of podzolization, a process that promotes SOC stability at depth. 

The retreat of the Mendenhall glacier has resulted in a unique opportunity to study incipient soil development from exposed granitic glacial till. 3 sample sets will be collected along the glacial forefield representing approximately 5 years of development and early pioneer species establishment. 6 additional sample sets, 3 per study area, will be collected in well-developed Spodosol soils of granitic origin at Taku Harbor and Prince of Wales Island representing mixed, mature forests with variable litter chemistry (i.e., western hemlock vs western red cedar) under increased precipitation and landscape age due to successive glacial retreat. Sample sites at these study areas are designed to capture local soil heterogeneity and differences in plant community composition. The sites also correspond to the field areas of an ongoing, multiyear incipient mineral weathering study established by our team. 

Analyses through the MONet initiative will complement the project’s objectives, providing site-specific context and critical insight into how soil properties (i.e., texture, total C:N, pH, pore network structure), bulk soil nutrient composition (i.e., geochemistry, total bases, CEC), and microbial community dynamics (i.e., metagenomics, potential enzyme activity, microbial biomass C and N) change along a bioclimatic weathering gradient. The findings of this work will advance our understanding of biological controls on global carbon cycling, improve climate modelling through bioweathering quantification, and increase the accuracy of soil carbon stock estimations.
results.title: Assessing the bioweathering of minerals along a bioclimate gradient

results.name: Soil mineralogy control on SOC stability in soils
results.description:
Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) pools and stability are influenced by interactions between climate, management, and soil properties. Numerous studies have determined the size and stability of SOC pools by incubation and other analytical methods. Few studies have linked the stability of SOC pools to soil clay mineralogy. However, these studies have not directly linked the stability of the SOC pools to the interactions between the SOC and soil mineralogy at molecular and structural configurations. Understanding these interactions at such scales offers not only a fundamental understanding of factors controlling SOC stability but means to upscale the stability of SOC pools to field, regional and continental scales by utilizing the spatial distribution of major soil minerals (smectite, kaolinite and mixed mineralogy) and climate gradient. 
The objectives of this research are to (i) investigate the soil mineralogy control on SOC stability in soils at a molecular scale and (ii) elucidate on the potential to map the SOC stability using spatial distribution of soil mineralogy and other soil properties, that are currently available for the U.S. In the best-case scenario soil cores with low and high OC and clay representing three major soil mineralogy classes for a total of 12 samples will be analyzed. Alternatively, 6 cores representing three major mineralogy classes with low and high OC will be analyzed. Priority will be given to sites associated with research network stations such as Long-Term Agro-Ecosystem Research (LTAR). The proposed research project will benefit from the MONet soil program that offers state of the art measurement methods and database facilities to support multiscale approaches for assessing the SOC stability. The research is a multipurpose collaborative effort that includes several partners such as DOI-BER, USDA-ARS, and DOE-PNNL.
results.title: Soil mineralogy control on SOC stability in soils

results.name: Ricketts MONet Request
results.description:
Switchgrass is a potential bioenergy feedstock and has adapted to a wide range of environments by exhibiting a variety of trait combinations that has resulted in multiple ecotypes across its range. The most divergent ecotypes are the uplands and lowlands, locally adapted to the northern and southern plains, respectively. Morphological trait differences between upland and lowland ecotypes exist and contribute to survivability in a range of environments. Aboveground, uplands typically produce relatively higher numbers of short, thin stems with higher nitrogen concentrations, while lowlands produce fewer, taller, thicker stems with lower nitrogen concentrations. Belowground, uplands have more fibrous, finer root structure compared to lowlands which have courser, thicker roots. Additionally, our recent publication (Ricketts et al. 2023, GCB Bioenergy) shows that the soil environment is equally, if not more, important than climate in determining switchgrass biomass yield. Therefore, to better understand (1) how variations in the soil environment affect switchgrass growth, and (2) the effects of switchgrass production on soil health and sustainability, we aim to quantify the differences in soil structural, physical, chemical, and biological characteristics resulting from the growth of two divergently locally adapted switchgrass ecotypes grown across their native range in the United States.

We propose to collect soil samples from 3 sites across a latitudinal gradient from Illinois to Texas where 6mx6m plots of switchgrass have been established for ~7 years. The soil types differ substantially among the sites, where the Mundelein silt loam at Fermilab, IL is a somewhat poorly drained mollisol, the Mexico silt loam in Columbia, MO is a poorly drained alfisol (with a relatively shallow claypan), and the Houston Black clay in Temple, TX is a moderately well-drained, slowly permeable vertisol that exhibits notable cracking during dry periods. We will collect 7 “events” at each site (>10m distance from one another); 3 from the upland Blackwell cultivar, 3 from the lowland Kanlow cultivar, and 1 from a plant-free control zone. All samples will be collected during peak plant growth relative to each site. 

The data obtained from the MONet soil program will provide us with information relevant for understanding the relationships between edaphic factors, belowground plant traits, and aboveground biomass yield in different environments. Additionally, it will provide crucial belowground context for various data collections obtained throughout the first 7 years of this project. For instance, X-ray Computed Tomography will help us to understand if/how differences in root traits affect soil pore network structure; FT-ICR-MS will help to identify potential differences in soil carbon inputs from the two ecotypes; microbial biomass data will enable us to better interpret 16S rRNA amplicon relative abundance data between sites; and the metagenomics and soil enzyme data from these root-associated bulk soil samples will supplement previously collected rhizosphere samples taken from these same plots to analyze microbial functional capacity. Overall, this data will provide us with a broader contextual framework for understanding plant-soil-microbial interactions in switchgrass and inform how genotype-by-environment (GxE) interactions might affect soil carbon dynamics/sequestration potential.
results.title: Ricketts MONet Request

results.name: Muscarella MONet Request
results.description: Wildfire frequency and intensity are increasing across Alaska, and the legacy of wildfire is associated with increased permafrost thaw and changes in forest composition. We hypothesize that wildfire legacy is linked to changes in soils, microbial communities, and their functions. As part of the Bonanza Creek LTER (BNZ), we are establishing post-burn sites to study wildfire legacy in boreal ecosystems. One of these sites is the Lost Horse Creek Fire, which is in the Caribou Poker Creek Research Watershed. This wildfire started in August 2023 and reached a peak of 9,317 acres. In addition, the burn area included a reburn of the 2021 Haystack Fire. To study this wildfire legacy, the BNZ is installing plots at three locations in the burn area: burned, reburned, and unburned. These transect plots are part of the larger ten-year Combustion, Climate, and Establishment experiment to study wildfire legacy. As part of the MONet soil program, we would submit 3 soil cores from each transect (9 soil cores total). Each plot has three subplots that will be monitored for soil and microbial characteristics as part of the CCE program. Inclusion in the MONet soil program will provide valuable data immediately after burns (<90 days) and will be used as the baseline to compare future data. The ability to sample and characterize these sites with the breadth of data included in MONet would fill a critical information gap that would help us meet our goal of understanding how wildfire legacy shapes the trajectory of ecosystem recovery in boreal ecosystems.
results.title: Muscarella MONet Request

results.name: Baggs MONet Request: The effects of agricultural nitrogen fertilization regimes on soil geochemistry
results.description:
Agriculture impacts the environment through several biogeochemical cycles that are relevant at local to global scales. To efficiently obtain high yielding harvests farmers are required to use management practices such as the input of synthetic fertilizers. However, synthetic fertilizers are not sustainable due to the high CO2 cost of production, requirements for non-renewable resources and unintended ecological impacts (eutrophication, water pollution). Understanding the complex environmental and resource outcomes of agricultural management decisions is extremely challenging due to the plethora of interacting factors. At Sound Agriculture we are developing science driven solutions for sustainable crop production. Our central question of interest is how does a proprietary chemical microbial activator and commercial practice synthetic Nitrogen fertilization regimens affect soil geochemistry over a field season.

We would plan to sample several plots from a single field at the start of the season before sowing and then again after harvest. One of three different treatments will be applied to each plot; 1. commercial practice N fertilization (150-220lb N/acre) , 2. 25lb/ac less than commercial practice N fertilization 3. 25lb/ac less than commercial practice N fertilization with microbial stimulants. Our proposal for the MONET call would be to have 3 collection events in May and then a further 3 collection events in September at the point of harvest. At each time point one collection event will be taken at each of the three fertilization treatments being studied. From our selected sites we will be working with farmers to gather additional data including AMF colonization of roots, shoot and root Nitrogen and Phosphorous stress marker gene expression and yield. Combined with the data from MONet this should help us to begin to unravel how management practices are affecting soil biogeochemistry and microbiome structures. Of particular interest is how the microbiome and the nutrients that they exchange with plants are affected by the fertilization regime through an agricultural field season. For instance we would like to understand how activating the microbiome compares to synthetic nitrogen in altering the flux of soil organic carbon, Nitrogen, Phosphorus and other rare minerals. Our field sample qPCR and microscopy data will allow us to see whether the differences in soil geochemistry and microbiome are visible in planta transcriptional reprogramming. Further understanding of soil chemistry and plant-microbe interactions will help us to fine tune how to promote plant growth whilst maintaining a healthy ecosystem. Through understanding the differences in nutrient flux overtime and between treatments we hope to gain a better understanding of what factors vary on this time scale and can be markers of healthy soils. We can additionally use yield data from our sites to see if there are any correlations between microbial or biogeochemical factors and yield. Finally we would like to query how management practices and the soil microbiome affect Mineral Associated Organic Matter and whether differences are perceptible over a crop season. Such information will help to inform future strategies for the integration of carbon credits into the agricultural economy.

results.name: Linking biotic drivers of soil structure to solute flows through soil profiles
results.description: Recent work highlights the powerful role that biota (here, roots and the microbes that surround them) play in governing soil structure over timescales much shorter than previously assumed. If robust across ecosystems, this observation suggests that the rapid response of biota to anthropogenic forcings (e.g., land use change, climate change) may impose yet-faster changes to soil structure in the Anthropocene. Such changes have great import for flows of water, nutrients, and dissolved organic carbon through soil profiles, and thus for ecosystem productivity and soil carbon fates. As part of a suite of projects at multiple sites in the U.S. funded by the NSF and the USDA, we seek participation in EMSL’s MONet project to provide detailed descriptions of soil properties in select locations and thus aid in hypothesis testing (see below). We propose to collect cores for MONet analyses at two established research sites: Coal Creek in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, and Reynolds Creek in Idaho. At these sites, we already have quantified rooting depth distributions every 1 cm to the base of the accessible profile. At Coal Creek, ongoing research quantifies soil [CO2] and [O2], soil moisture and temperature, and sapflux from canopy dominants. The graduate student who will benefit from MONet data has a funded project at Coal Creek exploring the role of transpiration-induced soil water movement in governing spatial heterogeneity of dissolved organic carbon; MONet data will aid in his data interpretation. At Reynolds Creek, ongoing research is probing the role of juniper encroachment into sagebrush stands in modifying soil water and carbon dynamics. There, we are currently generating the same rooting depth distributions already obtained for Coal Creek, and soil pits will be instrumented in late May 2023. The graduate student who will benefit from MONet data is quantifying the rates of aggregate formation and collapse in a lab setting; MONet data will help her expand her work to a field setting. At both places, basic soil chemistry and physical attributes have been quantified and assays to quantify aggregate size distributions are in process. We seek to augment our understanding of biotic influences on soil attributes via MONet data. Specifically, we hypothesize that because high relative abundances of roots and microbes are linked to relatively plentiful dissolved organic C and microbial necromass, in these locations we see promotion of relatively large soil aggregates and greater microporosity. We further hypothesize that these structural features are linked to greater hydrologic flow from surface horizons down-profile, resulting in greater depth distribution of surface horizon dissolved organic C. We therefore predict that MONet-provided soil hydraulic properties will exhibit a greater propensity for water flow where mean aggregate diameters (which we will quantify) are larger, that these tendencies will be exhibited more so where roots and microbes (and possibly FTICR and amino sugar estimates of necromass) are more abundant, and that organic matter characteristics will reveal a greater abundance of material similar in characteristics to surface material at depth than where flow rates are more tempered by smaller pores. Probing these hypotheses depends on controlling for soil texture and depth. At each site, we will sample soil cores representing a gradient of rooting types: at Coal Creek, from forest into meadow, and at Reynolds Creek from juniper-dominated into sagebrush-dominated. If our hypotheses appear valid, we will have demonstrated the importance of root and microbial abundances to soil structure for governing water and solute flows, features that until now have been studied in disparate fields. An alternative hypothesis is that root and associated microbial turnover results in pore clogging to a greater extent than macroporosity generation. With either outcome, the work will advance our ability to project how well-documented, human modification of ecosystem rooting depths, and thus of the depth distributions of rhizosphere microbial communities, can alter soil structural characteristics critical for ecosystem water, nutrient, and carbon flows. Please note that this abstract contains more information than the research proposal itself due to word limitations.
results.title: Linking biotic drivers of soil structure to solute flows through soil profiles

results.name: Ward Jones MONet Request
results.description:
Climate warming is benefitting high latitude agriculture by increasing air temperatures and the growing season length. However, permafrost (perennially frozen ground) thaw is accelerating and causing cascading effects to ecosystems and communities. Cultivating on permafrost-affected soils with high ground-ice content can lead to field abandonment as melting ground ice causes the land surface to collapse, also known as subsidence.  Permafrost Grown is a transdisciplinary project co-producing with Alaskan farmers to understand the interactions between agricultural practices and permafrost. We are focusing on current in-the-ground farming, as well as assessing the legacy effects of cultivated fields that were abandoned due to permafrost thaw and the socioeconomic trade-offs of cultivating on permafrost-affected soils. 
     Our project methods include sensor networks, characterizing permafrost conditions using geophysics and borehole sampling, agricultural experiments and cultivar testing, surveys, interviews, economic risk modelling, and unmanned arial vehicle (UAV) based remote sensing to monitor plant health throughout the growing season as well as to monitor ground surface subsidence and snow depth. Our project goals include creating decision-making tools for farmers, including best-practice guides and management strategy resources for cultivating on permafrost-affected soils to support sustainable agriculture in high-altitude regions.
     For the MONet program we propose to collect three to five samples within the active layer (thawed layer above permafrost) at five farms, four in Fairbanks and one in Two Rivers, Alaska, to address the following research questions:
(1) How do active layer soil properties change with varying land clearing histories (1950s to 2021), cultivation activities and underlying permafrost soil conditions?
(2) How does subsidence change soil properties that limit further farming practices?
(3) How do permafrost management strategies change soil properties? 
	All sites will have a sample collected within forested areas adjacent to farming activities. We will also collect six samples dedicated to cultivation types chosen to represent historically important Alaskan products: potato crop (replicated at two farms), peonies (two different ages at one farm), and brome hay (replicated at two farms). Three samples related to land clearing, one that was cleared in 2001 but never cultivated and the forest is regrowing, two for an area cleared in 2021, one sample will be collected in an area that is subsiding and the other in a non-subsiding area. Three samples collected in areas abandoned due to subsidence and four samples related to subsidence management, two in areas that subsided and were subsequently graded and infilled with soil and the other experimentally testing an asparagus crop (established in 2022) planted in an area that was always cultivated (previously potatoes) and extending the row in an area that was previously abandoned due to subsidence. 
      Participating in the MONet program will provide new data for our project that complements current and planned data collection. Abandoning whole or parts of fields is one of the most common problems related to permafrost thaw facing farmers participating in the Permafrost Grown Project. We are particularly interested in using the MONet data to help us understand how subsidence causes cultivation abandonment and begin to evaluate management strategies.

results.name: Biogeochemical controls on dissolved organic carbon production and degradation in tidal marshes
results.description:
The overarching objective of our ongoing research is to determine environmental (biotic and abiotic) controls on organic matter (OM) production and decomposition in tidal marsh soils along an estuarine salinity gradient. The proposed field locations represent tidal marsh systems that vary in elevation, hydrology, salinity, plant and microbial communities, soil characteristics, and biogeochemistry. This presents an ideal opportunity to measure and identify variables that may be responsible for OM production and decomposition. 

Tidal marshes are important components of the coastal carbon cycle due to their high productivity and carbon storage potential as well as their role in OM processing and export to adjacent waters. Most work to-date has focused on marsh surface waters even though belowground environments may be as equally important for OM processing and export. However, constraining the role of belowground OM in the coastal carbon cycle and in coastal carbon budgets has been difficult due to spatiotemporal differences in OM source and chemical composition, microbial community composition and function, and interactions between OM and microbial communities in soils and their porewaters. 

To address our objectives, a coupled geochemical-microbiological approach is necessary to assess the metabolic processes and functional groups responsible for OM production and decomposition in relation to OM characteristics and other biogeochemical parameters. Data obtained from the MONet soil program would support our goals to couple these approaches by providing high resolution data on soil properties (e.g., composition, geochemistry, C and N) as well as information about the microbial community (e.g., metagenomics, biomass, potential enzyme activity). These data would also complement existing bulk measurements related to dissolved OM concentration, source, and composition in tidal marsh porewaters. 

The proposed field locations and the subsequent data collected will provide information for the predictive understanding of soil processes that can be integrated into Earth system models and compared against other land types. This is especially critical along estuarine salinity gradients where soil processes are also traditionally thought to occur along a gradient (e.g., methane production decreases from freshwater to saltwater systems). However, gradients in salinity may not necessarily correlate to gradients in biogeochemical processes.
results.title: Biogeochemical controls on dissolved organic carbon production and degradation in tidal marshes

results.name: Midgley MONet Request
results.description:
Using a series of mature, mono-specific forestry plots, our collaborative team here at The Morton Arboretum together with our partners outside the Arboretum are addressing interdisciplinary questions regarding tree responses to climate change; relationships among leaf, stem, root and mycorrhizal phenology; forest carbon and nutrient dynamics; and the connections among tree traits, soil invertebrate and microbial communities, and soil biogeochemistry. The specific sites used in our study were intentionally selected to include wide phylogenetic and functional diversity among tree species ensuring relevance of our findings to ecosystem processes across northern hemisphere temperate forests and ready incorporation into terrestrial biosphere models (e.g., Wang et al. 2023). To address our questions, we developed a comprehensive platform for long-term monitoring of leaf, stem, and root growth; growth of mycorrhizal fungi and repeated sampling of mycorrhizal communities; soil respiration; and stem and sap flow. We then couple these observations with ongoing monitoring of abiotic conditions including soil moisture, temperature, electrical conductivity, and standard meteorological measurements. We have also conducted intensive sampling campaigns assessing invertebrate communities, root exudation rates, tree demography, ecosystem nutrient budgets, and specific soil properties associated with individual species (Midgley and Sims 2020).

For our proposed sampling with the Molecular Observation Network (MONet), we will focus on a series of 11 mono-specific sites, all under the same climate conditions within the 690-hectare Arboretum grounds. The 11 sites are roughly evenly split between angiosperms and gymnosperms and within each group, split between both arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal associating species, with additional stratification across our two dominant soil types, Alfisols and Mollisols. MONet therefore provides an opportunity for us to better link tree species effects to soil and ecosystem properties. We are particularly interested in gaining greater insights into the organic matter fractions among our sites as well as detailed soil hydraulic properties and pore network structure. Furthermore, we expect the metagenomics data and enzyme activity will closely complement our planned sampling and analysis of mycorrhizal fungal communities among our sites. We further propose to repeat our sampling at two time points. The first sampling will take place during the typical growing season (June/July). The second sampling will be outside of the typical growing season after fall leaf senescence occurs in deciduous species (October/November). We are selecting this second date as our previous observations indicate this to be an important period of growth for both roots and mycorrhizal fungi across our sites. We therefore expect changes in many of the properties assessed by MONet, especially metagenomics, enzyme activity, and respiration.

results.name: Soil Function Across Variably Inundated Environments - Tidal Systems
results.description: We aim to generate knowledge, data, and models that are transferable across Earth’s variably inundated ecosystems. We are focused on the integrated hydro-biogeochemistry of soils in these diverse systems. Of particular interest is understanding how inundation history shapes the physical, chemical, and biological environment and how those components jointly lead to emergent biogeochemical fluxes, including shifts in fluxes in response to altered inundation states. In this proposal we are targeting sites that experience variable inundation due to tides. The objective is to generate a foundational dataset for comparative analyses of the physical-chemical-biological environment and how that integrated environment is related to fluxes (e.g., CO2 production). We further aim to leverage the large number of MONet samples across soil environments that may not be variably inundated. By merging data from systems that are and are not variably inundated we can evaluate the hypothesis that the physical-chemical-biological environment of all variably inundated systems clusters near soil systems from wet/humid regions (and away from arid soils). This is a starting hypothesis and characterization effort ultimately aimed at generating refined hypotheses to guide follow-on sampling and modeling efforts. In addition, our collective team plans to submit additional MONet proposals to cover other types of variably inundated environments. These will include hillslopes with surface runoff, non-perennial streams, temporary ponds, wetlands, floodplains, coastal systems inundated due to storms, and soil systems engineered to enable specific/controlled inundation regimes.
results.title: Soil Function Across Variably Inundated Environments - Tidal Systems

results.name: Berens MONet Request
results.description:
Natural and anthropogenic stressors are rapidly altering biogeochemical processes in coastal soils. Efforts to model these changes are limited by the availability of data that capture the complex interactions of salinity, hydrology, sediment, and nutrients. Our scientific objective is to evaluate how hydrologic gradients in coastal wetlands undergoing degradation or growth influence biogeochemical processes and regulate carbon and nutrient cycling.
This research targets a total of seven sample sets across one prograding and one degrading delta system (coastal land cover type) in Louisiana, USA (Southeastern ecoregion). Four sample sets (sets 1–4) will be collected from the Wax Lake Delta, a prograding freshwater delta comprised of islands that span gradients of soil age (~0–60 yrs since deposition) and exhibit distinct ecological zones based on soil elevation relative to a tidal datum. One sample set will be collected from two ecological zones (supratidal and intertidal; ~10 m apart) of two soil transects (younger soils and older soils; ~1 km apart) on Mike Island. The intertidal zones experience microtidal oscillations (<0.3 m) and are inundated less than half of the time. Sensors installed at sites 1–4 continuously record soil redox potential, salinity, pH, and water level. Surface and porewater samples (0–50 cm below ground surface) are being collected ~3–4 times per year and analyzed for geochemical parameters including dissolved organic and inorganic carbon, trace elements (e.g., Fe, Mn, P, Al), base cations, and major inorganic anions and nutrients (i.e., Cl-, SO42-, NO3-, PO43-, soluble reactive P, NH4+).
Three sample sets (sets 5–7) will be collected from Terrebonne Bay, a degrading delta system comprised of organic-rich wetlands that span a salinity gradient, reflective of sea level rise and saltwater intrusion. Soils will be collected along a 20 km transect from sites influenced by saline, brackish, or freshwater. Sites 5–7 are near Coastwide Reference Monitoring System (CRMS) stations that record data on water (salinity, water level), vegetation (classification, biomass), and soil properties (organic content, bulk density).
Participation in the MONet program will support our goals by providing biogeochemical and microbial data using analytical tools not available in our laboratory and that complement our ongoing field research on the Louisiana Gulf Coast. Together, these data will fill a significant knowledge gap and aid inclusion of coastal wetland ecosystems into Earth system models. Our seven sample sets provide a space-for-time continuum of coastal soils experiencing either degradation and seawater encroachment or potential growth from restoration projects that will each be critical for parameterizing multiscale Earth system models used to simulate and predict changes in ecosystem processes and services in future climate scenarios.
results.title: Berens MONet Request

results.name: Cheeke MONet Request
results.description: The Palouse prairie is an endangered ecosystem in Eastern Washington and Northern Idaho which is highly fragmented. Remaining Palouse prairie remnant habitats are threatened by annual grass invasion, particularly annual grass Ventenata dubia. To investigate the impacts of V. dubia invasion on above- and below-ground communities, including arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, we set up field plots (4 x 4 meters within a 50 x 50 m area separated by at least 5 m) on Smoot Hill (WA, USA) in areas with high percent cover of V. dubia (invaded plots), intermediate percent cover of V. dubia (transition plots), and low percent cover of V. dubia (native plots). We have collected data on plant community composition, percent cover of biological soil crusts, and mycorrhizal fungal inoculation potential from each plot. Through the MONet soil program, we aim to submit samples from three replicate field plots from three invasion levels (3 native plots, 3 transition plots, 3 invaded plots = 9 plots total) to better understand how soil biotic and abiotic properties may change with V. dubia invasion. With this information, we will be able to gain insights into how V. dubia invasion may affect soil processes and microbial metabolic activity in an endangered prairie. This information will also help us understand if restoration of soil biota communities is necessary after V. dubia invasion to restore soil function. Finally, data from the MONet soil program will inform our future experiments aimed at restoration of the Palouse prairie habitat on Smoot Hill and at other sites within the Palouse prairie bioregion.
results.title: Cheeke MONet Request

results.name: Examining the role of hydraulic redistribution on seasonal shifts to biogeochemical and physical properties of the subsurface.
results.description: Hydraulic redistribution (HR) is the passive movement of water within the soil profile via biological pathways (namely roots and fungal hyphae) from wetter areas to drier areas. The translocation of water from deep soil to the upper soil horizons may have important intra- and inter-annual implications on root morphology, soil-biologic activity, solute transport, carbon stability dynamics, and soil physical and structural properties. We seek to elucidate how hydraulic redistribution may alter soil physical and biological properties, as well as nutrient dynamics, in what would otherwise be two very similar hillslopes. To explore this, we have chosen sites on two adjacent hillslopes within the HJ Andrews Experimental Forest which have been shown, through previous study, to experience two contrasting hydraulic redistribution regimes: high HR activity, and little to no HR activity. It is hypothesized that differences in the relative magnitude of HR, even within high- and low-HR plots, are a result of variation in groundwater accessibility to surface vegetation, and to trees in particular. Three sampling events separated temporally have been chosen to highlight changes that occur at each site across an entire period of seasonal drought. The MONet soil program will allow us to analyze changes in soil physical properties, carbon dynamics, and biologic activity associated with the near surface soils that are most impacted by the influx of redistributed water. Core and sample collection for the MONet soil program will occur alongside existing efforts at each site to map the magnitude, location, geometry, and flow paths of near surface water using state-of-the-art geophysical techniques. Combined, the MONet soil program and existing research efforts at the sites will provide important insight into the dynamic soil processes associated with variable water accessibility under drought conditions.
results.title: Examining the role of hydraulic redistribution on seasonal shifts to biogeochemical and physical properties of the subsurface.

results.name: Tolar MONet Request
results.description: We seek to understand wetland soil processes along a gradient within our local Cape Fear River from fresh, non-tidal wetlands to fresh and oligohaline tidal wetlands, to more saline marshlands closer to the mouth of the river. The PIs working with this dataset comprise a microbial ecologist specializing in biogeochemical cycling (Tolar), a wetland ecologist specializing in soil carbon (Sutter), and a biogeochemist specializing in metabolites (Johnson). As pre-tenure faculty at UNCW, we are beginning our research programs and focusing on study sites we can monitor into the future and observe how predicted changes will impact both microbial and plant communities, as well as their associated biogeochemical processes and chemical exchanges. The MONet program would provide an incredible resource for comparison to other similar sites across the continental US, as well as an otherwise challenging to obtain comprehensive data for our own samples that would form the basis for future proposals and collaborations. This dataset also partners nicely with proposals we will submit this year examining carbon flux with incoming salinity changes along this gradient. We view these studies as complementary, where MONet would provide the structure to base future work and sampling, and potentially concurrent sampling if awarded other external grants. For the samples proposed here, our primary research objectives include: 1) comparison of microbial- and plant-driven ecosystem function across similar sites with distinct salinity and tidal conditions, 2) determination of key metabolites and osmolytes produced and exchanged between plants and microbes at each site, and 3) seasonal shifts in carbon flux to form a baseline for future changing conditions in this region.
results.title: Tolar MONet Request

results.name: Investigating interactions between soil microbial communities and soil organic matter dynamics along climate and vegetation gradients
results.description: Soils hold globally-important stocks of organic matter, with critical relevance for nutrient cycling and climate change. As the primary agents of decomposition, soil microbes play a key role in soil organic matter (SOM) turnover. However, the complexity of interactions among the physical, chemical and biological properties of soil challenges efforts to characterize the mechanisms that control SOM dynamics over space and time. Our proposed project will draw on National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) soil samples from across the US, using EMSL and JGI facilities to better understand the mechanisms controlling SOM persistence within and across ecosystems, by linking SOM chemistry with soil metabolomics, metaproteomics and metagenomics. Soil samples and data from the NEON Biorepository will be complemented by existing data and samples from an ongoing SOM stabilization mechanism study using NEON soils. Using these diverse samples, we will characterize SOM composition and the microbial metabolite profile using FTICR, GC-MS, and solid- and liquid-state NMR, and we will characterize soil microbial genetic potential and proteins using untargeted metagenomics and metaproteomics. We will test for the relative importance of specific microbial traits associated with SOM persistence by determining the genes and proteins associated with the mechanisms of SOM persistence, as characterized within the NEON datasets and our ongoing study. We will link SOM composition with the microbial metabolite profile, determining how metabolite classes and target metabolites reflect chemical, physical, or biological controls on SOM, and how the strength of these controls is influenced by environmental stress. Together, our proposed analyses will apply the powerful analytical capabilities of EMSL and JGI to the extraordinary datasets and samples afforded by the NEON network, bolstered by the samples from the mechanistic experiments within our ongoing experiment, to probe emerging paradigms of SOM persistence. Our findings will support predictions of continental SOM stabilization under future global change, as well as improving our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms underpinning SOM dynamics.
results.title: Investigating interactions between soil microbial communities and soil organic matter dynamics along climate and vegetation gradients
